text.p: Turkey's triple Olympic weightlifting champion Naim Suleymanoglu has announced he is retiring from the sport.
"All these championships, records, medals -- I am now 30 -- this is enough," Suleymanoglu said. "I am now leaving the sport never to return."

Turkish weightlifting federation chairman Savas Agaoglu applauded the decision. "I am glad he has given up at the peak," Agaoglu said on Friday. "Naim did not have any more targets after turning all records upside down for 19 years."
Suleymanoglu, who won his third consecutive Olympic gold in Atlanta last year, said he had nothing more to prove.
"There could now only be one aim and that was the Sydney Olympics. But I cannot actively stay in the sport for another four years," Suleymanoglu said.
Suleymanoglu, who visibly struggled in Atlanta to beat off the challenge from Greece's Valerios Leonidis, said that after a long rest he hoped to become a weightlifting coach or administrator.
The former trainer of the national team Enver Turkileri said Suleymanoglu should now be appointed technical director of the national squad.
Born Naim Suleimanov in the small Bulgarian mountain village of Ptichar, Suleymanoglu's life and career encapsulated the tortured ethnic conflicts of eastern Europe.
He won the world junior championship at 14 for Bulgaria, at 15 set a world record and at 16 he became only the second man to lift three times his bodyweight.

Although he initially enjoyed great luxury in Bulgaria -- earning a flat and a living allowance some three times the national average -- he soon became the target of Sofia's forced assimilation of ethnic Turks.
The authorities banned Moslem holidays and burials, according to rights groups, and Turks were forced to change their names -- Suleymanoglu became Naum Shalamanov.
That was the last straw and Suleymanoglu defected to Turkey during the 1986 world championships in Melbourne.

Ankara handed over an estimated $1 billion to Bulgaria and Suleymanoglu won Turkey's first Olympic gold in 20 years at the 1988 Seoul Olympic Games. He retained his title in Barcelona and won numerous world and European titles.
His success spawned a sporting revolution in Turkey, which thanks to other ethnic Turkish imports from Bulgaria has become a force on the world weightlifting scene.

Suleymanoglu now lives in Ankara, where his brother is the national team coach. His father, a zinc miner, and his mother, who worked in a greenhouse, were brought to Turkey in the wake of his defection after much diplomatic effort by Ankara.
Following his dramatic defection Bulgaria allowed a third of the nation's 900,000 Turks to emigrate to Turkey.
